lesson.menu_title: What the Song Is Really Saying
lesson.menu_desc: A song on the car radio, a chorus you misheard for years, and the grammar to tell someone what the singer says: he said he was leaving, she promised to wait -- 35 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 5 -- What the Song Is Really Saying
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Cauê de França | Lesson 5 -- What the Song Is Really Saying
lesson.grammar_point: reported speech: tense backshift (is leaving > was leaving, will > would, have never > had never), time words, and reporting verbs (admit, explain, promise, warn, tell)

listenings.text: Good evening, it's ten past nine, and here's a song that's been on everybody's lips this month. I spoke to the singer last week, and he told me a great story. He said he had written it on a night bus, after a really bad day at work. He explained that the first line came to him while he was looking out of the window. He admitted that he had never expected it to be a hit. In fact, he said his band almost didn't record it. And when I asked him about the fans, he promised he would play it at every concert, even when he gets tired of it. So here it is. Sing along if you know the words.

Okay, confession time. For about ten years, I was sure that a famous rock song had a line about a bathroom. It doesn't. Not even close. And I'm not alone. Almost everybody mishears lyrics, and there's a good reason. Singers stretch the words to fit the melody, the drums are loud, and our brain does what brains do. It fills the gaps with words it already knows. That's why learners mishear even more. So here's my advice. Pick a song you love, look up the lyrics, read them once, and then listen again. Try to make out each word. You'll be amazed how much you missed, and how quickly it gets better.

I teach music, but half of my students come to me to learn English. And songs really work. Think about the chorus. You hear it four, five, six times in one song. That's free repetition, and you don't even notice it. Then there's the melody. A catchy melody gets stuck in your head, and the words come with it. One of my students told me last year that she had learned more English from songs than from her grammar book. I believed her. What about slang? Don't worry about it at first. Sing along, enjoy it, and look it up later. Trust me, it'll grow on you.
